summary: How a RADAR times and builds each pulse, shares 1 antenna between sending and listening, and powers it all.

blocks.title: Timing
items: Synchronizer, also the timer or triggering section: operation of any RADAR begins here.
The timer sets the PRR and range markers, and sends blanking and unblanking signals to the CRT.
Single-swing blocking oscillator: gives accurate timing pulses, short and sharp.

blocks.title: Modulator
items: Modulator: gives the magnetron high-voltage pulses of the proper shape and width: the correct waveform.
Switch: a thyratron or SCR, silicon-controlled rectifier. Both latch on, then turn off once the PFN is empty.
PFN, pulse forming network: an artificial delay line, or transmission line, of series inductors and shunt capacitors. It sets the pulse's shape and duration.
Pulse modulation: RF in short bursts. Modulation frequency is the PRR: 60 to 500 Hz.
Resonant charging choke: lets the pulse exceed the supply voltage, reducing high-voltage supply requirements. A diode holds the charge.

blocks.title: Magnetron facts
items: Magnetron: the transmitter in a marine RADAR.
High voltage goes on the cathode, so the anode can stay at ground potential.
Rise time relates to accurate range measurement: range is timed from the leading edge.

blocks.title: Duplexer
items: Duplexer: an electronic switch that lets 1 antenna transmit and receive.
Keep-alive: DC on the TR tube. It partially ionizes the gas, making the tube more sensitive.
Ferrite circulator: the duplexer's usual part; it replaces the TR cell. The ferrite is a phase shifter.
Circular cavity, flat ends: E-lines are perpendicular to the end walls.

items.name: Directional coupler
items.means: Every 10 dB is a factor of 10.

blocks.title: Power supplies
items: High voltage supplies deliver DC to charge the PFN. Low voltage supplies may give AC and DC.
Switching regulator: its switch is fully on or off, so overall efficiency is much higher than linear.
PWM, pulse-width modulator: varies the duty cycle of the regulator switch to control the output voltage. Frequency stays fixed.
Pulse width increases when the load impedance decreases.
FET: on compares to a pure resistor, off to a mechanical relay.
Power MOSFET: high input impedance; failure mode is gate punch-through.

items.def: pulse repetition rate, pulses per second.

blocks.title: Exam traps
items: Not part of the transmitting system: the klystron, the receiver's local oscillator.
False statement: high voltage supplies over 5,000 volts AC.
Triggering section is also known as the synchronizer, not the timer.
Unblanking pulses go to the CRT.
ATR keeps echoes out; TR protects and mutes. "All of the above" is wrong there, but right for the timer.
Pulse bigger than the supply: a resonant charging choke, not a voltage multiplier.
